children: OTTAWA--Canadian inflation remained elevated but steady last month, with little sign the spike in energy costs this year is sparking wider price pressures

The consumer-price index slipped 0.1% in August and the annual rate was unchanged at 3%, Statistics Canada said Monday. That leaves inflation at the top end of the 1%-to-3% window the Bank of Canada aims for following July's slight acceleration.

Measures of underlying inflation continued to be more subdued despite some stress on consumer wallets from higher rents and travel-related costs in August. For most economists, that suggests the Bank of Canada can remain on the sidelines for now as it watches for a second-round of inflation sparked by high oil prices.

Gasoline prices fell during the month and were up less sharply compared with a year earlier than they were in July. That meant a nearly 23% year-over-year rise at the pumps versus the roughly 26% jump a month prior. Stripping out gasoline, the consumer price index rose a six-month high 2.4% in August after July's 2.2% advance, speeding up in part due to an acceleration in costs for travel tours thanks to comparisons with last year when far fewer Canadians traveled to the U.S. which put downward pressure on air fares and other travel prices.
The trimmed mean and weighted median measures of core inflation preferred by the Bank of Canada were unchanged, averaging 1.95% annually.

The scope of inflation also remained relatively benign, with economists noting about 35% of components in the CPI basket showed inflation above 3%, down slightly from a month earlier and well below last fall when roughly half of the components were tracking above 3%.
Rents were higher in Canada last month, but consumers paid less for clothing than a year ago and grocery prices for the first time in two years rose by less than headline inflation.

]The lack of inflation breadth may give the central bank some comfort that the impact of higher oil prices is still contained, though crude has jumped again in the last week as tensions in the Middle East have escalated.

"The benign starting point for core inflation will allow Canadian officials to be more patient than some of their global counterparts, but the Bank of Canada will also be forced into action if crude prices don't come down in the coming weeks. For monetary policy, oil is now in the driver's seat," said Royce Mendes, head of macroeconomic strategy at Desjardins.

The central bank will have one more inflation report before next deciding on interest rates in late October, though markets currently are pricing in a roughly 75% chance of an increase at the coming meeting. The

bank earlier this month again left its policy rate unchanged but officials remain wary of inflation risks the longer the Iran war continues and as new U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-measures are imposed on trade between the two countries.
The rise in fuel prices will likely push up headline inflation, but the outlook for core inflation remains more subdued, KPMG Canada's senior economist Peter Shannon said.

"Our analysis suggests pass-through from higher fuel prices is limited and concentrated in the most directly exposed items, while there are minimal signs of demand-driven inflation pressures throughout the CPI basket," he said.

For Shannon and others the expectation remains the Bank of Canada will leave rates on hold for the foreseeable future, particularly given heightened trade and tariff uncertainty, though not all economists agree. Some economists pointed to the trim and median measures of CPI that rose 0.2% on a monthly basis, while traditional core inflation that excludes food and energy was 3.9% month-over month in annualized terms, the hottest since April 2025.
"These numbers," said Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Bank of Nova Scotia, "are strongly suggesting that the Bank of Canada is behind the curve in fighting inflation."
